l: touch, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Sixth Lecture.
s: Touch is one of the five aspects of development. Things which develop with regard to touch are of eight kinds: hard, soft, heavy, light, cold, hot, smooth, and rough.

l: figure, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Sixth Lecture.
s: Figure is one of the five aspects of development. Things which develop with regard to figure are of five kinds: globular, circular, triangular, square, and long.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: This unit explains the division of Living Beings into perfected souls (siddhas) and beings still belonging to the Samsâra. It describes perfected souls, their abode at the top of the world, and their qualities, then classifies immovable and movable beings, including Earth Lives, Water Lives, plants, Fire Lives, Wind Lives, animals, men, denizens of hell, and gods. It also gives durations, bodily continuance, varieties, and habitats for many classes. The unit concludes with religious exercises, Bhâvanâs, conditions affecting Bôdhi and rebirth, and the teaching of Gñâtri(putra) in the Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana.

l: Living Beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Living Beings are divided into those still belonging to the Samsâra and perfected souls (siddhas). Those still belonging to the Samsâra are movable or immovable, with numerous subdivisions.

l: Samsâra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: The Samsâra contains living beings that have not reached perfection. Perfected souls have crossed its boundary and are rid of transmigration.

l: perfected souls (siddhas), Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Perfected souls include women, men, hermaphrodites, orthodox, heterodox, and householders. They reside at the top of the world, have no visible form, consist of Life throughout, and possess knowledge, faith, and incomparable happiness.

l: Îshatprâgbhâra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Îshatprâgbhâra is the place twelve Yôganas above Sarvârtha where perfected souls go. It is shaped like an open umbrella, consists of white gold, and is forty-five hundred thousand Yôganas long and broad.

l: Sarvârtha, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Sarvârtha is the Vimâna above which Îshatprâgbhâra is located. In the great Vimâna Sarvârtha(siddha), the duration of life is always thirty-three Sâgarôpamâs.

l: world (Lôka), Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: The world contains the places where living beings exist and from which perfected souls are not debarred. Perfected souls reside at its top, while the subtile Earth Lives, Water Lives, and plants are distributed all over it.

l: Ginas, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: The best of the Jinas are said to have described Îshatprâgbhâra as resembling an open umbrella.

l: life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Perfected souls consist of Life throughout. Life is also discussed through the durations of the various living beings and their bodies.

l: knowledge, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Perfected souls are developed into knowledge. Those well versed in sacred lore and possessing much knowledge are worthy to hear the doctrine of salvation.

l: faith, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Perfected souls are developed into faith. Orthodox opinions and faith in the creed of the Ginas are associated with reaching Bôdhi and escaping the Circle of Births.

l: immovable living beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Immovable living beings are of three kinds: Earth Lives, Water Lives, and plants. Each kind is divided into subtile and gross forms, which may be fully developed or undeveloped.

l: Earth Lives, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Earth Lives are subtile or gross, and fully developed or undeveloped. Gross and fully developed Earth Lives include smooth and rough varieties, and their duration, bodies, intervals, and varieties are described.

l: Water Lives, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Water Lives are subtile or gross, and fully developed or undeveloped. Gross and fully developed Water Lives include pure water, dew, exudations, fog, and ice.

l: plants, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Plants are subtile or gross, and fully developed or undeveloped. Gross and fully developed plants either share one body or each possess its own body, and their kinds and durations are described.

l: Fire Lives, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Fire Lives are subtile or gross, and fully developed or undeveloped. Gross and fully developed Fire Lives include coal, burning chaff, fire, flame of fire, meteors, and lightning.

l: Wind Lives, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Wind Lives are subtile or gross, and fully developed or undeveloped. Gross and fully developed Wind Lives include squalls, whirlwinds, thick winds, high winds, low winds, and the Samvartaka wind.

l: animals, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Movable beings with organic bodies are animals divided into those possessing two, three, four, or five organs of sense. Their kinds, habitats, durations, and bodily continuance are described.

l: beings with five organs of sense, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Beings with five organs of sense are denizens of hell, animals, men, and gods. The unit describes their subdivisions, habitats, and durations of life.

l: denizens of hell, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Denizens of hell are divided according to seven hells called Ratnâbha, Sarkarâbha, Vâlukâbha, Paṅkâbha, Dhûmâbha, Tamâ, and Tamatamâ. Their shortest and longest durations increase according to the hell in which they live.

l: gods, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Gods are of four kinds: Bhaumêyikas, Vyantaras, Gyôtishkas, and Vaimânikas. Their subdivisions and durations of life are described, including the Kalpas, Graivêyakas, and Anuttaras.

l: Bhâvanâs, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: The Kandarpa-, Abhiyôgika-, Kilvisha-, Môha-, and Asuratva-Bhâvanâs lead to evil ways and are obnoxious at the time of death. Their practices include ribaldry, spells, reviling sacred beings, anger, prognostics, and prohibited acts.

l: Bôdhi, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Souls with heretical opinions, sins, and killing do not reach Bôdhi at death. Souls with orthodox opinions, no sins, and white Lêsyâ reach Bôdhi at death.

l: Circle of Births, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: Those who love and practise the creed of the Ginas become pure and free from passions and eventually get out of the Circle of Births.

l: Gñâtri(putra), Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: The enlightened and liberated Gñâtri(putra) delivered the Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana.

l: Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, B. Living Beings.
s: The Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana were delivered by the enlightened and liberated Gñâtri(putra). The pious approve of them.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: This unit concerns the descent, conception, and transfer of the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, the last of the Tîrthakaras. Mahâvîra first took the form of an embryo in the womb of Devânandâ in the brahmanical part of Kundagrâma, but Sakra ordered Harinegamesi to transfer him to the womb of Trisalâ in the Kshatriya part. Devânandâ saw fourteen great dreams, and Rishabhadatta interpreted them as signs that she would bear a remarkable son. The text also states that Mahâvîra's descent, conception, transfer, birth, renunciation, and attainment of Kevala occurred under Uttaraphalgunî, while his final liberation occurred under Svâti.

l: Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Mahâvîra is the Venerable Ascetic and the last of the Tîrthakaras. He descended from the great Vimâna Pushpottara, took the form of an embryo in Devânandâ's womb, and was later transferred to Trisalâ's womb.

l: Brâhmanî Devânandâ, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Devânandâ is a Brâhmanî of the Gâlandharâyana gotra and the wife of Rishabhadatta. She saw the fourteen great dreams and first carried Mahâvîra's embryo in the brahmanical part of Kundagrâma.

l: Sakra, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Sakra, chief and king of the gods, perceived Mahâvîra's conception through Avadhi. He ordered Harinegamesi to transfer Mahâvîra from Devânandâ's womb to Trisalâ's womb because Tîrthakaras are born in high families.

l: Harinegamesi, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Harinegamesi is the divine commander of the foot troops. At Sakra's command, he transferred Mahâvîra's embryo from Devânandâ's womb to Trisalâ's womb and placed Trisalâ's embryo in Devânandâ's womb.

l: Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Trisalâ is a Kshatriyânî of the Vâsishtha gotra, wife of Siddhârtha. Her womb received Mahâvîra's embryo when Harinegamesi carried out Sakra's command.

l: the Arhats, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The Arhats are revered in the opening obeisances and in Sakra's praise. Sakra reflects that Arhats are born in high, noble, royal, or similarly pure families, not in low or brahmanical families.

l: the Ginas, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The Ginas are praised as conquerors who have conquered fear, reached the path of perfection, and are liberated and liberators.

l: the Tîrthakaras, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The Tîrthakaras are praised as perfectly enlightened guides and benefactors of the world. Mahâvîra is identified as the last of the Tîrthakaras, following twenty-three earlier Tîrthakaras.

l: the gods, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The gods include Sakra and the divine beings under his command. They enjoy permitted divine pleasures, and Harinegamesi uses divine motion and transformation to carry out Sakra's order.

l: Gambûdvîpa, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Gambûdvîpa is the continent where Mahâvîra's conception and embryo transfer take place. It contains Bharatavarsha and the town of Kundagrâma.

l: Bharatavarsha, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Bharatavarsha is the region within Gambûdvîpa where Kundagrâma is located and where Mahâvîra takes the form of an embryo.

l: Kundagrâma, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Kundagrâma is the town in Bharatavarsha where Mahâvîra is conceived. Its brahmanical part contains Devânandâ's house, and its Kshatriya part contains Siddhârtha and Trisalâ's house.

l: the brahmanical part of Kundagrâma, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The brahmanical part of Kundagrâma is where Devânandâ and Rishabhadatta dwell. Mahâvîra's embryo is first placed there and is later removed from it.

l: the Kshatriya part of Kundagrâma, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The Kshatriya part of Kundagrâma is where Siddhârtha and Trisalâ dwell. Harinegamesi places Mahâvîra's embryo in Trisalâ's womb there.

l: Uttaraphalgunî, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Uttaraphalgunî is the asterism joined with the moon during Mahâvîra's descent, conception, embryo transfer, birth, renunciation, and attainment of Kevala.

l: Mahâvîra's descent from heaven, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Mahâvîra's descent from heaven occurred when the moon was in conjunction with Uttaraphalgunî. He descended from the Vimâna Pushpottara after his divine existence had reached its termination.

l: Mahâvîra's conception, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Mahâvîra's conception occurred in the middle of the night under Uttaraphalgunî. He first took the form of an embryo in the womb of Devânandâ.

l: the transfer of Mahâvîra's embryo, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The transfer of Mahâvîra's embryo occurred on Sakra's command, in the middle of the night under Uttaraphalgunî. Harinegamesi moved it from Devânandâ's womb to Trisalâ's womb and exchanged it with Trisalâ's embryo.

l: birth of Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Mahâvîra's birth is stated to have occurred under Uttaraphalgunî. The unit does not describe the birth itself.

l: Mahâvîra's renunciation, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Mahâvîra's renunciation, when he tore out his hair, left the house, and entered houselessness, is stated to have occurred under Uttaraphalgunî.

l: Kevala, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Kevala is the highest knowledge and intuition obtained by Mahâvîra under Uttaraphalgunî. It is described as infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and perfect.

l: Mahâvîra's final liberation, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: Mahâvîra's final liberation occurred under Svâti. The unit does not provide further details about that event.

l: the fourteen great dreams, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The fourteen great dreams were seen by Devânandâ while between sleeping and waking. They were an elephant, bull, lion, the anointing of Srî, a garland, moon, sun, flag, vase, lotus lake, ocean, celestial abode, heap of jewels, and flame.

l: embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra (in Trisalâ's womb), Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The embryo of Trisalâ was placed in the womb of Devânandâ when Harinegamesi transferred Mahâvîra's embryo to Trisalâ's womb.

l: the womb of Devânandâ, Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra / Lives of the Ginas. / Life of Mahâvîra.
s: The womb of Devânandâ first received Mahâvîra's embryo. Harinegamesi later removed Mahâvîra's embryo from it and placed the embryo of Trisalâ there.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was removed
s: This unit concerns the removal of the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra from the womb of the Brâhmanî Devânandâ and its transfer to the womb of the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ. Afterward, Trisalâ sees fourteen auspicious dreams, including an elephant, bull, lion, goddess Srî, garland, moon, sun, flag, vase, lotus lake, milk-ocean, celestial abode, heap of jewels, and fire. She awakens joyful after seeing them. The text states that every mother of a Tîrthakara sees these fourteen dreams when the famous Arhat enters her womb.

l: Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was removed
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra is the person whose embryo is removed from the womb of the Brâhmanî Devânandâ and transferred to that of the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ.

l: Brâhmanî Devânandâ, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was removed
s: The Brâhmanî Devânandâ of the Gâlandharâyana gotra carries the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra until it is removed from her womb. While in a state between sleeping and waking, she sees the fourteen dreams being taken from her by the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ and awakens.

l: Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was removed
s: The Kshatriyânî Trisalâ of the Vâsishtha gotra receives the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra into her womb. She then sees fourteen illustrious, beautiful, lucky, blest, auspicious, fortunate, great dreams and awakens with the hair of her body bristling for joy.

l: embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra (in Trisalâ's womb), Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was removed
s: The embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra is removed from the womb of the Brâhmanî Devânandâ and placed in the womb of the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ.

l: the fourteen great dreams, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was removed
s: The fourteen dreams of the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ are an elephant, bull, lion, goddess Srî, garland, moon, sun, flag, full vase, lotus lake, milk-ocean, celestial abode, heap of jewels, and fire. They are described as fine, beautiful, lovely, handsome, and auspicious.

l: mothers of Tîrthakaras, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was removed
s: The text states that every mother of a Tîrthakara sees these fourteen dreams on the night in which the famous Arhat enters her womb.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, When the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, having seen these fourteen illustrious, great drea
s: Kshatriyânî Trisalâ tells Kshatriya Siddhârtha about fourteen illustrious great dreams, and he interprets them as foretelling the birth of a son who will become either a universal emperor or a Gina. Interpreters of dreams confirm this interpretation from their dream-books before Siddhârtha and Trisalâ. The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra remains motionless in the womb to spare his mother anxiety, later moves, and resolves not to enter the state of houselessness during his parents’ lives. After nine months and seven and a half days, Trisalâ gives birth to a healthy boy, Mahâvîra.

l: Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, Kalpa Sutra, When the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, having seen these fourteen illustrious, great drea
s: She awakens after seeing fourteen illustrious great dreams and asks Kshatriya Siddhârtha what they portend. She accepts his interpretation and that of the interpreters of dreams, then returns to her apartments. She carries her unborn child carefully and gives birth to a perfectly healthy boy.

l: Siddhârtha, Kalpa Sutra, When the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, having seen these fourteen illustrious, great drea
s: He interprets Trisalâ’s fourteen dreams as foretelling a lovely son who will become a brave king, a universal emperor, or a Gina. He summons the interpreters of dreams, hears their confirmation, honours them, and tells Trisalâ the interpretation.

l: Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, When the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, having seen these fourteen illustrious, great drea
s: He is brought into the family of the Gñâtris, after which the family’s wealth, possessions, power, and glory increase, leading his parents to resolve to name him Vardhamâna. He remains motionless in the womb to spare his mother anxiety, then moves when he learns of her sorrow. He resolves not to enter the state of houselessness during his parents’ lives and is later born as a perfectly healthy boy.

l: interpreters of dreams, Kalpa Sutra, When the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, having seen these fourteen illustrious, great drea
s: They are summoned by Kshatriya Siddhârtha and come to his palace after performing auspicious rites. They consult their knowledge, recite the dream-books, and explain that Trisalâ’s fourteen dreams foretell a universal emperor or a Gina. Siddhârtha honours them with gifts and dismisses them.

l: the fourteen great dreams, Kalpa Sutra, When the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, having seen these fourteen illustrious, great drea
s: They are seen by Kshatriyânî Trisalâ and are interpreted as portending the birth of a son who will become a universal emperor or a Gina. The interpreters of dreams identify them as fourteen great dreams associated with the mothers of universal monarchs or Arhats.

l: dream-books, Kalpa Sutra, When the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, having seen these fourteen illustrious, great drea
s: They enumerate forty-two common dreams and thirty great dreams. They state that the mothers of universal monarchs or Arhats see fourteen of the thirty great dreams when such an embryo enters the womb.

l: birth of Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, When the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ, having seen these fourteen illustrious, great drea
s: After the lapse of nine months and seven and a half days, in the first month of summer and during the dark fortnight of Kaitra, Trisalâ gives birth in the middle of the night to a perfectly healthy boy while the moon is in conjunction with Uttaraphalgunî.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: This unit recounts the birth, naming, renunciation, ascetic practice, attainment of Kevala, and final liberation of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra. His parents named him Vardhamâna, while the gods gave him the name Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra. He abandoned his property, entered houselessness, endured hardships for more than twelve years, and attained Kevala during his thirteenth year. He later died in Pâpâ, became a Siddha, Buddha, and Mukta, and his disciple Indrabhûti attained Kevala that same night.

l: Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born in Kundapura and belonged to the Kâsyapa gotra. He renounced his property and kingdom, practiced asceticism and meditation, attained Kevala, established a large community, and finally died in Pâpâ after becoming liberated.

l: Vardhamâna, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: Vardhamâna was the name given to the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra by his parents because their wealth and possessions increased after his birth.

l: Indrabhûti, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: Indrabhûti, the oldest disciple of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra and a monk of the Gautama gotra, cut asunder his tie of friendship for his master on the night of his master's death and attained Kevala.

l: Sramanas, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: Sramanas are described as ascetics, and the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was called Sramana because he was devoid of love and hate. After the great Graha called Kshudrâtma entered his natal asterism, less respect and honour would be paid to Sramanas, Nirgrantha monks, and nuns until it departed.

l: Kundapura, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: Kundapura was the town where the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born. King Siddhârtha ordered it to be decorated, cleaned, supplied with festivities, and filled with performers and celebrations for the birth.

l: birth of Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: At the birth of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, divine lustre appeared, gods and goddesses caused great confusion and noise, and riches were rained upon king Siddhârtha's palace. His parents celebrated the birth and named him Vardhamâna.

l: Mahâvîra's renunciation, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra perceived that the time for renunciation had come and abandoned his wealth, kingdom, army, household, and other possessions. In the park called the Shandavana of the Gñâtris, he removed his ornaments, plucked out his hair, and entered the state of houselessness.

l: Mahâvîra's attainment of Kevala, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: After meditating for twelve years, the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra attained the highest knowledge and intuition called Kevala during his thirteenth year. He became a Gina, Arhat, and Kevalin, omniscient and comprehending all objects and conditions of living beings.

l: Nirvâna of Mahâvira, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra died in king Hastipâla's office of the writers in Pâpâ during the last night of the rainy season. He cut asunder the ties of birth, old age, and death and became a Siddha, Buddha, Mukta, and finally liberated being.

l: fourfold Karman, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra exerted himself to suppress the defilement of Karman. At his death, the Karman producing Vedanîya, Âyus, name, and family had been exhausted.

l: Kevala, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: Kevala is described as infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and full knowledge and intuition. The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra attained it during his thirteenth year, and Indrabhûti attained it on the night of Mahâvîra's death.

l: Mahâvîra's final liberation, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra obtained final liberation after dying in Pâpâ. He was freed from all pains and became a Siddha, Buddha, and Mukta.

l: Law of the Sramanas, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: The Laukântika gods urged the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra to establish the religion of the law benefiting all living beings. During his renunciation, he was also urged to defend the conquered Law of the Sramanas.

l: state of houselessness, Kalpa Sutra, In that night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born, there was a divi
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra entered the state of houselessness after leaving his home and tearing out his hair. He later walked naked, accepted alms in the hollow of his hand, guarded his thoughts, words, and acts, and endured pleasant and unpleasant occurrences with equanimity.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, (147) Since the time that the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died, &c.
s: The unit states that nine centuries have elapsed since the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died. It adds that the eightieth year of the tenth century has been reached, though another redaction gives the ninety-third year. The Fifth Lecture ends, as does the Life of Mahâvîra.

l: Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, (147) Since the time that the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died, &c.
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira is stated to have died. Nine centuries have elapsed since his death, and the text records the eightieth year of the tenth century, with another redaction giving the ninety-third year.

l: Nirvâna of Mahâvira, Kalpa Sutra, (147) Since the time that the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died, &c.
s: The death of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira is used as the point from which the elapsed centuries and years are counted.

l: nine centuries, Kalpa Sutra, (147) Since the time that the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died, &c.
s: Nine centuries are said to have elapsed since the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died.

l: eightieth year, Kalpa Sutra, (147) Since the time that the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died, &c.
s: The eightieth year is identified as the current year of the tenth century since the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died. Another redaction gives the ninety-third year instead.

l: Fifth Lecture, Kalpa Sutra, (147) Since the time that the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died, &c.
s: The Fifth Lecture ends in this unit.

l: Life of Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, (147) Since the time that the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died, &c.
s: The Life of Mahâvîra ends in this unit.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: This unit recounts the Life of Pârsva, including his descent and conception, birth, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, and final liberation. Pârsva was born in Benares, lived thirty years as a householder, then entered houselessness with three hundred men. He attained Kevala after eighty-four days and later died on mount Sammeta after a hundred-year life, becoming freed from all pains. The asterism Visâkhâ marked the five most important moments of his life.

l: Pârsva, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Pârsva was an Arhat and the people's favourite. He lived thirty years as a householder, eighty-three days in a state inferior to perfection, something less than seventy years as a Kevalin, and fully seventy years as a Sramana, living one hundred years in all.

l: Sramanas, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Pârsva instituted an excellent community of sixteen thousand Sramanas with Âryadatta at their head. He also had three hundred and fifty sages who knew the fourteen Pûrvas and other groups of Sramanas with specified attainments.

l: Benares, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Benares was the town in Bharatavarsha where Pârsva descended, was conceived, and was born. Pârsva later traveled through Benares to the park called Asramapada when he renounced the household life.

l: Visâkhâ, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Visâkhâ was the asterism in conjunction with the moon during Pârsva's descent and conception, birth, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, and final liberation. These were described as the five most important moments of his life.

l: Kevala, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Kevala was the infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and full highest knowledge and intuition. Pârsva attained it under a Dhâtaki tree on the eighty-fourth day after entering houselessness.

l: final liberation, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Pârsva obtained final liberation when the moon was in conjunction with Visâkhâ. He later died on the summit of mount Sammeta, freed from all pains.

l: descent and conception, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Pârsva descended from the Prânata Kalpa after living there for twenty Sâgaropamas. He then took the form of an embryo in the womb of Vâmâ, wife of Asvasena, king of Benares.

l: birth of Pârsva, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: After nine months and seven and a half days, Vâmâ gave birth to a perfectly healthy boy. Pârsva was born in Benares on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Paushya, with the moon in conjunction with Visâkhâ.

l: renunciation of Pârsva, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Pârsva renounced the household life in the second month of winter, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Paushya. After fasting three and a half days, he tore out his hair with three hundred men and entered the state of houselessness.

l: attainment of Kevala, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Pârsva attained Kevala on the eighty-fourth day after entering houselessness. He fasted two and a half days without drinking water and reached the highest knowledge and intuition under a Dhâtaki tree.

l: death of Pârsva, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Pârsva died on the summit of mount Sammeta after fasting a month without drinking water. His death occurred during the light fortnight of Srâvana, with the moon in conjunction with Visâkhâ, and he was freed from all pains.

l: Life of Pârsva, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: The Life of Pârsva describes his descent, conception, birth, household life, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, community, epochs, death, and final liberation. It states that twelve centuries had elapsed since his death and that the thirteenth century was in its thirtieth year.

l: houselessness, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Pârsva.
s: Pârsva entered houselessness after tearing out his hair and remained there for eighty-three days before attaining Kevala. During this period he neglected his body, was circumspect, and meditated upon himself.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: The Life of Arishtanemi recounts the major events in the life of the Arhat Arishtanemi, whose five most important moments occurred under the asterism Kitrâ. It describes his descent, birth, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, community, lifespan, death on mount Girnâr, and final liberation. It also records the numbers of his followers and the time elapsed since his death.

l: Life of Arishtanemi, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: The Life of Arishtanemi recounts his descent from heaven, birth, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, teachings, death, and final liberation.

l: Arhat Arishtanemi, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: The Arhat Arishtanemi descended from the Vimâna Aparâgita, was born in Sauripura, renounced the world with a thousand persons, and attained Kevala under a Vetasa tree on mount Girnâr. He had eighteen Ganas and eighteen Ganadharas, along with large communities of Sramanas, nuns, lay votaries, and sages.

l: Arishtanemi's birth, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: Arishtanemi took the form of an embryo in the womb of queen Sivâ, wife of king Samudravigaya, in Sauripura. After nine months and seven and a half days, Sivâ gave birth to a perfectly healthy boy named Arishtanemi.

l: Arishtanemi's renunciation, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: Arishtanemi renounced the world in the park Revatîka after fasting for two and a half days without drinking water. Under the asterism Kitrâ, he tore out his hair with a thousand persons and entered the state of houselessness.

l: mount Girnâr, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: On mount Girnâr, Arishtanemi attained infinite knowledge and intuition called Kevala under a Vetasa tree. He later died on its summit after fasting for a month without drinking water, in the company of five hundred and thirty-six monks.

l: Kevala, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: Arishtanemi attained the highest knowledge and intuition called Kevala on the fifty-fifth day after his renunciation. He lived something less than seven centuries as a Kevalin.

l: Sramanas, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: The Arhat Arishtanemi had an excellent community of eighteen thousand Sramanas with Varadatta at their head. He also had four hundred sages who knew the fourteen Pûrvas, fifteen hundred Avadhi-knowing sages, fifteen hundred Kevalins, and other groups of sages and disciples.

l: Arishtanemi's death, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: Arishtanemi died on the summit of mount Girnâr in the middle of the night when the moon was in conjunction with Kitrâ. He fasted for a month without drinking water and died in a squatting position surrounded by five hundred and thirty-six monks.

l: final liberation, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Arishtanemi.
s: After his fourfold Karman was exhausted, Arishtanemi was freed from all pains and obtained final liberation. Since his death, eighty-four thousand years and part of the eighty-fifth millennium had elapsed.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras.
s: The unit describes the epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras and calculates elapsed years from the deaths of Arhat Nami, Munisuvrata, and Malli. It states that 584,979 years have elapsed since Arhat Nami died, that the current year is 1,184,980 since Munisuvrata’s death, and that it is year 6,584,980 since Malli’s death. It places Sîtala’s death a krore of Sâgaropamas less 42,003 years and eight and a half months before Vîra’s death. It also gives increasingly remote intervals separating earlier Tîrthakaras from Sîtala and Malli.

l: Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras, Kalpa Sutra, Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras.
s: The epochs record elapsed years since the deaths of Arhat Nami, Munisuvrata, and Malli, and give chronological intervals between several Tîrthakaras. They include the relative dates of Sîtala, Vîra, and earlier Tîrthakaras.

l: Arhat Nami, Kalpa Sutra, Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras.
s: Arhat Nami’s death is used as a chronological starting point. Since his death, 584,979 years have elapsed, and this is the eightieth year.

l: Munisuvrata, Kalpa Sutra, Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras.
s: The chronology states that the current year is 1,184,980 since Munisuvrata’s death.

l: Malli, Kalpa Sutra, Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras.
s: The chronology states that the current year is 6,584,980 since Malli’s death. Ara died 10,000,000 years before Malli, while Kunthua, Sânti, Dharma, Ananta, Vimala, Vâsupûgya, and Sreyâmsa died progressively earlier by the intervals specified.

l: Sîtala, Kalpa Sutra, Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras.
s: Sîtala died a krore of Sâgaropamas less 42,003 years and eight and a half months before the death of Vîra. Suvidhi, Kandraprabha, Supârsva, Padmaprabha, Sumati, Abhinandana, Sambhava, and Agita died the stated numbers of krores of Sâgaropamas before Sîtala.

l: Vîra, Kalpa Sutra, Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras.
s: Vîra’s death is used as the reference point for Sîtala’s death. Sîtala died a krore of Sâgaropamas less 42,003 years and eight and a half months before Vîra.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: This unit recounts the life of the Arhat Rishabha, the Kosalian, from his descent from heaven and conception to his birth, reign, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, death, and final liberation. Rishabha taught sciences, accomplishments, arts, and occupations during his reign, then anointed his hundred sons as kings before entering houselessness. He attained Kevala after prolonged austerities and meditation, established a large fourfold community, and ultimately died on mount Ashtâpada after fasting. The unit ends by relating the elapsed time from Rishabha’s death to the death of Mahâvîra.

l: Rishabha, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha, the Kosalian, was an Arhat of the Kâsyapa gotra and had five names: Rishabha, First King, First Mendicant, First Gina, and First Tîrthakara. He lived eight millions four hundred thousand years on the whole, established a large fourfold community, and was ultimately freed from all pains.

l: Sramanas, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha had an excellent community of eighty-four thousand Sramanas with Rishabhasena at their head. He also had twenty thousand male disciples who had reached perfection and twenty-two thousand nine hundred sages in their last birth.

l: Kevala, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha reached the highest knowledge and intuition called Kevala after fasting three and a half days, engaging in deep meditation, and attaining infinite knowledge.

l: Mahâvîra's descent from heaven, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha descended from the great Vimâna called Sarvârthasiddha after living there for thirty-three Sâgaropamas. His descent occurred in the dark fortnight of Ashâdha on its fourth day, when the moon was in conjunction with Uttarâshâdhâ.

l: conception of Rishabha, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: After descending from heaven, Rishabha took the form of an embryo in the womb of Marudevî, wife of the patriarch Nâbhi. Marudevî saw dreams, including a bull coming forward with his face, and Nâbhi himself interpreted them.

l: birth of Rishabha, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Marudevî gave birth to a perfectly healthy boy, Rishabha, in the dark fortnight of Kaitra on its eighth day. The circumstances connected with his birth were otherwise the same as those of Mahâvîra, except that the contents of §§ 100 and 101 did not apply.

l: reign of Rishabha, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha lived six millions three hundred thousand former years as a king. During his reign he taught the seventy-two sciences, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men, and he anointed his hundred sons as kings, giving each a kingdom.

l: renunciation of Rishabha, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha left the town Vinîtâ for Siddhârtha Vana, tore out his hair with four thousand royal persons and Kshatriyas, and entered the state of houselessness. He began this renunciation in the first month of summer, in the dark fortnight of Kaitra on its eighth day.

l: attainment of Kevala, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: After neglecting his body and meditating upon himself for one thousand years, Rishabha fasted three and a half days and attained Kevala outside Purimatâla, in the park called Sakatamukha, under the tree Nyagrodha.

l: death of Rishabha, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha died on the summit of mount Ashtâpada in the company of ten thousand monks, after fasting six and a half days without drinking water. His death occurred in the dark fortnight of Mâgha on its thirteenth day, when the moon was in conjunction with Abhigit.

l: final liberation, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha obtained final liberation when the moon was in conjunction with Abhigit. After his fourfold Karman was exhausted, he was freed from all pains.

l: life of Rishabha, Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha.
s: Rishabha lived two millions of former years as a prince, six millions three hundred thousand former years as a king, and together eight millions three hundred thousand former years as a householder. He then lived a thousand former years in a state inferior to perfection and ninety-nine thousand former years as a Kevalin, for a total life of eight millions four hundred thousand years.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: This unit concerns the lineage of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, beginning with his nine Ganas and eleven Ganadharas. It describes the deaths of the Ganadharas and states that the present Nirgrantha Sramanas descend spiritually from Ârya-Sudharman. It then lists successive Sthaviras and their disciples, Ganas, Sâkhâs, and Kulas in short and detailed redactions. The unit concludes with reverences to later teachers, including Gambû, Nandita, Desiganin, Sthiragupta, Dharma, and Devarddhi.

l: Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra had nine Ganas and eleven Ganadharas. He was of the Kâsyapa gotra, and his lineage is traced through successive Sthaviras.

l: Indrabhûti, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: Indrabhûti of the Gautama gotra was the oldest monk of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra and instructed five hundred Sramanas. He died after the Nirvâna of Mahâvira.

l: Ârya-Sudharman, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: Ârya-Sudharman of the Agnivesyâyana gotra instructed five hundred Sramanas and was one of the two Ganadharas who died after the Nirvâna of Mahâvira. The Nirgrantha Sramanas of the present time are described as his spiritual descendants.

l: Ganas, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra had nine Ganas. Later Ganas, including those founded by Godâsa, Uttara and Balissaha, Rohana, Bhadrayasas, Kâmarddhi, Srîgupta, Rishigupta Kâkandaka, and Susthita and Supratibuddha, are described with their Sâkhâs and Kulas.

l: Ganadharas, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra had eleven Ganadharas, who knew the twelve Aṅgas, the fourteen Pûrvas, and the whole Siddhânta of the Ganins. They died after fasting for a month without drinking water, and the text states that the other Ganadharas left no descendants.

l: Nirgrantha Sramanas, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: The Nirgrantha Sramanas of the present time are all described as spiritual descendants of Ârya-Sudharman.

l: Sthaviras, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: The Sthaviras are presented as a succession of teachers beginning with Ârya-Sudharman and continuing through numerous named figures. Their disciples founded Ganas and Sâkhâs, preserved sacred lore, and were praised for knowledge, conduct, virtue, penance, patience, self-restraint, and clemency.

l: Nirvâna of Mahâvira, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: The Nirvâna of Mahâvira occurred before the deaths of the Sthaviras Indrabhûti and Ârya Sudharman. The Ganadharas died after the Nirvâna of Mahâvira.

l: Bhadrabâhu, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: Ârya Bhadrabâhu of the Prâkîna gotra had four disciples of the Kâsyapa gotra: Godâsa, Agnidatta, Ganadatta, and Somadatta. Godâsa founded the Godâsa Gana, which was divided into four Sâkhâs.

l: Sthûlabhadra, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: Sthûlabhadra of the Gautama gotra appears in the short redaction as a Sthavira after Ârya Sambhûtavigaya. In the detailed redaction, he is one of the twelve disciples of Ârya Sambhutavigaya.

l: Mahâgiri, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: Ârya Mahâgiri of the Ailâpatya gotra had eight disciples. Uttara and Balissaha founded the Uttarabalissaha Gana, while Khaluka Rohagupta founded the Trairâsika Sâkhâ.

l: Suhastin, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: Ârya Suhastin of the Vâsishtha gotra had twelve disciples. His disciples founded several Ganas and Sâkhâs, including the Uddeha, Uduvâtika, Vesavâtika, Kârana, Mânava, and Kautika Ganas.

l: detailed redaction, Kalpa Sutra, List of the Sthaviras.
s: The detailed redaction gives an expanded list of Sthaviras after Ârya Yasobhadra. It records their disciples and the Ganas, Sâkhâs, and Kulas associated with them, continuing through Ârya Sândilya.

l: Kalpa Sutra, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: This unit explains when the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra and later religious communities commence the Paggusan, and gives rules for conduct during it. It regulates residence, travel, alms collection, food and drink, permissions, clothing and utensils, cleanliness, lodging, speech, disputes, and movement. It also describes special dietary restrictions, precautions concerning small living beings and moisture, and practices intended to support monastic control. The unit concludes with Mahâvîra proclaiming the Lecture called Paryushanâkalpa and identifies itself as the end of the Rules for Yatis and of the Kalpa Sûtra.

l: Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra commenced the Paggusan when a month and twenty nights of the rainy season had elapsed. In the town of Râgagriha, in the Kaitya Gunasilaka, he proclaimed the Lecture called Paryushanâkalpa.

l: Paggusan, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The Paggusan is commenced after a month and twenty nights of the rainy season have elapsed, though it may be commenced earlier but not later. During it, monks and nuns follow detailed rules concerning residence, travel, alms, food, permissions, cleanliness, speech, lodging, and reconciliation.

l: rainy season, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The rainy season determines the customary commencement of the Paggusan after a month and twenty nights have elapsed. During it, living beings, grass, seeds, mildew, and sprouts frequently come forth, requiring monks and nuns to inspect places carefully.

l: Sthaviras, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The Sthaviras follow the conduct prescribed during the rainy season and are restricted during the Paggusan from asking householders about things they do not see. They also have specified rules concerning hair, lodging, and conduct.

l: Nirgrantha Sramanas, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The Nirgrantha Sramanas of the present time commence the Paggusan after a month and twenty nights of the rainy season have elapsed, following the example of earlier religious teachers.

l: monks, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: Monks during the Paggusan must observe rules governing residence, travel, alms collection, diet, permissions, bodily cleanliness, inspection of living beings and moisture, lodging, speech, disputes, and movement. They must often seek permission from a superior before undertaking ordinary activities and must maintain practices intended to support control.

l: nuns, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: Nuns during the Paggusan are subject to rules concerning residence, travel, alms, food, bodily cleanliness, inspection, lodging, speech, disputes, and movement. They must not accept food or drink for one who has not asked them or whom they have not promised to assist.

l: householders, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: Householders prepare and clean their houses before the customary commencement of the Paggusan. Converted and devoted householders honour, praise, and permit visits by monks, but are not to be prompted about things that are not seen because they might buy or steal them.

l: Âkârya, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: During the Paggusan, the Âkârya directs whether a sick brother may give or accept food. The Âkârya also gives instructions concerning required food for the sick and is among the superiors whose permission a monk must seek before various activities.

l: Paggusan dietary restrictions, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: Hale, healthy, and strong monks or nuns are not allowed frequently to take milk, thick sour milk, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, sugar, honey, liquor, and meat during the Paggusan. Rules also limit meals, drinks, donations, and alms visits according to the length of a monk's fast.

l: alms, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: During the Paggusan, monks and nuns collect alms under restrictions concerning distance, weather, timing, donations, permitted drinks, and permission from superiors. Food for a sick man may be accepted only in the quantity requested and not under false pretence.

l: Paggusan conduct rules, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The Paggusan conduct rules require careful inspection of places and substances, permission before leaving or undertaking activities, proper beds and benches, three pots, specified lodging places, notice of intended direction, and limits on travel. They prohibit harsh words, require forgiveness and reconciliation after disputes, and regulate conduct in rain and around householders.

l: Paryushanâkalpa, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The Paryushanâkalpa is the Lecture proclaimed by the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra. It is presented with its application, argumentation, information, text, meaning, and examination of meaning.

l: Kalpa Sûtra, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The unit ends by identifying itself as the end of the Kalpa Sûtra.

l: monastic control, Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis.
s: The rules of the Paggusan are intended to make monastic control easier through proper beds and benches, inspection and cleaning, restraint in speech and conduct, permission from superiors, reconciliation after disputes, and care to avoid harm to small living beings.

l: Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: This record summarizes Book I of the Akaranga Sutra, Hermann Jacobi’s translation of Sudharman’s discourse heard from Mahâvîra. Across eight lectures, it sets out a religious path of non-injury, restraint, renunciation, and liberation from karman and samsâra. The First Lecture teaches that humans and other beings possess souls, suffer birth, rebirth, and pain, and must renounce harm to earth-, water-, fire-, wind-, plant-, and animal lives. The Second through Fifth Lectures depict carelessness, attachment, desire, sensuality, wealth, ignorance, violence, and sinful acts as sources of grief and continued birth and death; they praise the wise, houseless sage who abandons possessions, controls passions, follows truth, and seeks the opposite shore. Righteousness is defined especially by refusing to slay, abuse, torment, or drive away any breathing, living, sentient creature. The text contrasts this teaching with claims of some Brâhmanas or Sramanas, while presenting the Seer and heroic sages as disciplined, equanimous, and free of worldly weakness. It also teaches that the Self is the knower and that the liberated has no body, qualities, or material conditions. The Sixth and Seventh Lectures turn to religious discipline: awakened teachers, monks, ascetics, disciples, householders, mendicants, food, illness, vows, penance, and religious death. They call for patience, abstinence, right faith, rejection of goods gained through injury or theft, endurance of pain, reduced food, and unwavering restraint so that karman may be dissolved and Nirvâna entered. The Eighth Lecture offers Mahâvîra as the culminating example. During thirteen years of wandering and meditation, he abandoned his robe and endured deprivation, attacks, abuse, cold, heat, and pain without seeking comfort or medical treatment. He carefully avoided harm to all forms of life and proceeded undisturbed toward Nirvâna.

l: Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Akaranga Sutra’s First Book opens with the First Lecture, Knowledge of the Weapon, teaching souls, sin, non-injury, self-control, and six kinds of lives across seven lessons.

l: Mahâvîra, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Mahâvîra is the Revered One, a Tîrthakara, wise Brahman, ascetic, and sage whose discourse Sudharman heard. He teaches comprehension and renunciation of sin’s causes, faith, the three vows, and a law for the instructed to follow. As a naked, houseless, world-relinquishing sage, he practices strenuous asceticism, nonviolence, careful eating, and avoidance of karman and sin. After one year and one month he gives up his robe, then wanders for thirteen years in meditation and severe self-control. Lodging in resting-places, he carefully begs, avoids medical treatment and shelter, and endures dogs’ attacks, hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and bodily pain without desire or disturbance, proceeding toward Nirvâna.

l: houseless, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Houseless is a desireless religious person who gives up the world, ceases to act, renounces desire, and wanders toward final liberation. They avoid unclean possessions and transactions, possess only code-permitted food, prescribed clothing, an alms-bowl, and examined straw for secluded rest. They do no harm to living beings, reject goods gained through killing, theft, force, or injury, restrain senses and bodily motion, and avoid sin through disciplined conduct. They speak little, meditate, endure pain and cold patiently, even rejecting fire, and practice penance and nonviolence. Following vows and limiting possessions, they continue contemplation, endure religious death without attachment to life or death, and seek Nirvâna and freedom from bonds.

l: men, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Men may control themselves or only pretend to be houseless. Sinful acts toward earth, water, fire, plants, animals, and wind cause loss of happiness and perfect wisdom. Attached to sense objects and lust, they suffer, fail to reach liberation, and come to destruction through frail bodies; when benighted, they are subject to old age and death. Seeing living beings suffer, they should lead a religious life: restrain themselves, recognize friendship, understand truth, overcome Mâra, and renounce causes of sin. Carelessness returns a man to life, but circumspect practice may bring liberation from death and make men reward-knowing sages.

l: living beings, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Living beings are individually embodied and include earth-, water-, fire-, and wind-bodies, plants and their growth, animals, people, and creatures such as crows, cats, and dogs. They are fond of life and pleasure, dislike pain and destruction, and experience both pleasant and unpleasant feelings, terror, unhappiness, and many forms of suffering. Their varied conditions, births, and miseries arise through action and karman; beings may harm one another and become sinners through their actions. Because pain is feared and disagreeable to every sort of living being, they must not be slain, violently treated, abused, tormented, disturbed, or harmed directly, through another, or through careless acts. The account culminates in careful recognition of life in ground, bodies, and the world: a monk should protect beings, and Mahâvîra avoids injuring them while wandering and begging.

l: Self, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The Self is presented as a soul believed to be born again and again. It is the knower or experiencer through which one knows. Denying the self denies the relevant living world, while maintaining the right doctrine of Self enables understanding of this teaching.

l: world, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The world is a realm of samsara in which desire brings repeated birth and death. Believed in by men, it includes beings, directions through which souls descend and wander, six classes of living beings, worldly pleasures and weakness, and many pains. It is afflicted, miserable, difficult to instruct, and without discrimination; it is a source of delusion, attachment, desire, carelessness, sensual enjoyment, passions, disease, violence, and the consequences of action. Living beings experience pleasures, pains, attachments, passions, and pleasant and unpleasant feelings, while love and hate connect the world with birth and sensation. The discerning and wise understand it as suffering, value it properly, cast off its idea and attachments, and avoid injurious work. A compassionate saint preaches the faith to the world in every direction.

l: sin, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Sin is action in the world that arises when one acts toward living bodies, causes or permits others to act, and includes injury, taking what is not given, and dealing in goods obtained through such acts. It arises through ignorance, carelessness, attachment, sensuality, and currents of sin; when not comprehended and renounced, it causes birth, rebirth, pain, and suffering. The teaching calls for comprehending, renouncing, avoiding, repenting of, and diminishing sin through care, penance, restraint, reduced food, guarded speech, and religious precepts. Mahâvîra exemplifies this by neither committing, inducing, nor consenting to sin.

l: karman, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Karman is owned by people through acknowledged acts and arises from the condition of living beings, sinful acts, desires, attachment to pleasures, and violence, especially killing. It causes birth, misery, pain, movement into various families, and pleasant or unpleasant consequences. The records urge understanding its roots and currents, fully knowing and renouncing injurious acts, observing commandments, cutting fetters and worldly connection, and restraining impulses. The wise ascetic subdues passions, endures hardships, remains unattached, practises prescribed methods and contemplation, and through penance, restraint, ascetic exertion, and destruction of sinfulness gets rid of karman.

l: samsâra, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Samsâra is a cycle or whirlpool of rebirth: birth and death, pain, worldly attachment, acts, karman, conception, and the misery of the world. Beings undergo manifold births, and those who acquiesce in or prefer worldly pleasures, remain attached, ignorant, or careless turn round and round in it, born again and again. Some do not know whether the soul is reborn, while others know it is. The wise, passionless sage or hero seeks freedom by renouncing desire and acts, discontinuing sin, and becoming enlightened. Crossing samsâra ends this course of births; the Seer has put an end to acts, worldly existence, and samsâra.

l: pain, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Pain is unpleasant, disagreeable, and greatly feared by living beings. It includes suffering, terror, unhappiness, and painful feelings, and harmful actions toward living bodies contribute to it. It arises through worldly pleasures, loss, bodily decay, sickness, birth and death, and a chain from wrath and delusion to hell; actions are its source. The afflicted fool remains caught in its whirl, while the wise avoid its causes and preach renunciation. Pain also appears as physical hardship from cold, fire, hunger, wounds, and attacks. Mahâvîra endured such pains without treatment, resentment, or attachment.

l: houselessness, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: requires self-control [as conduct of the houseless] Houselessness is associated with acting rightly, doing pious work, practising no deceit, and ceasing from works. Some men only pretend to be houseless while continuing harmful conduct.

l: self-control, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Self-control is a religious discipline associated with final liberation. Retained through an illustrious path, it prevents sinful harm toward living bodies through comprehension and renunciation. It unfolds as control that frees a person from attachment despite hardship, then as abstinence through which a sage destroys the effects of works, endures hardships, and brings about scarcity of wants or karman.

l: earth-bodies, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_living beings [individually embodied] Earth-bodies are individually embodied living beings that can be cut, struck, and killed. Injuring them is a sinful act that must be comprehended and renounced.

l: water-bodies, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Water-bodies are declared living matter containing many lives; monks teach that injuring them, including by using unstrained water, is sinful and takes what was not given.

l: fire-bodies, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_living beings [according to the doctrine] Fire is treated as a living body whose use can injure many beings. Beings living in earth, grass, leaves, wood, cowdung, dust-heaps, or near fire may shrivel, lose their sense, and die through contact with fire.

l: plants, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_like men [in birth, growth, illness, nourishment, decay, change and impermanence] Plants are living bodies that are born, grow old, fall sick when cut, need food, decay, change, and are not eternal. Injuring plants is a sinful act that must be comprehended and renounced.

l: animals, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_living beings [individually embodied] Animals are beings with different modes of production and experience pleasure, displeasure, pain, terror, and unhappiness. They are killed for sacrifices, skin, flesh, blood, bodily parts, or because they have harmed or may harm people.

l: wind-bodies, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_living beings [individually embodied] Wind is treated as a living body that can be injured by acts relating to wind. Beings near wind may fall into it, shrivel, lose their sense, and die.

l: aggregate of six kinds of lives, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: includes wind-bodies The aggregate of six kinds of lives consists of earth-bodies, water-bodies, fire-bodies, plants, animals, and wind-bodies. A wise man should not act sinfully toward it, cause others to do so, or allow others to do so.

l: religious faith, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_taught_by Mahâvîra [as the faith to be coveted] Religious faith is learned through Mahâvîra, the monks, or instruction, and is to be retained by those entering the order. It includes faith in the soul, the world, reward, action, and the path to final liberation.

l: final liberation, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Final liberation is a sought purpose, alongside birth and death, attained through self-control, renunciation, desirelessness, and cessation from action. It requires understanding and abandoning the causes of sin, property and its idea, violence, ignorance, sensuality, attachments, and injurious deeds. Those attached to sense objects or burdened by sin do not reach it. The houseless and hero advance by control and renunciation; the liberated, inactive person has no passage from birth to birth.

l: Knowledge of the Weapon, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Knowledge of the Weapon, the First Lecture containing First through Seventh Lessons, teaches that harming living bodies causes sin and must be understood and renounced.

l: Second Lecture, Called Conquest of the World, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_a lecture It teaches renunciation of worldly desires, possessions, violence, and carelessness. It praises control, non-killing, true knowledge, and the pursuit of final liberation.

l: monk, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: A monk is an ascetic who enters religious life before old age, renounces wealth, possessions, desire, aversion, and violence, and seeks final liberation. He knows the law and the world with right comprehension, is righteous, self-possessed, wise, just, chaste, and properly aware of sensual perceptions. He leads a mendicant life by collecting alms from all families and preaching the law to all creatures without injuring any being, including himself. He avoids killing and lying, practices carefulness and control, follows the commandment and, if not yet discriminating, follows the âkârya while examining his conduct. He patiently bears unpleasant feelings, heat and cold, pleasure and pain, hardship, abuse, injury, and reviling, regarding mistreatment as connected with former sins. Through equanimity, abstinence, and conquest of obstructions to righteousness, he abandons worldliness.

l: hero, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The hero is a person defined by disciplined self-control and knowledge. He endures the hardships of control, crosses life’s flood, liberates the fettered, and avoids attachment, discontent, lust, violence, pleasures, and bad works. Grounded in knowledge, he conquers wrath, pride, deceit, greed, and other passions, destroys sorrow, and remains careful and restrained. Along with other heroes, he follows the difficult road toward final liberation, where there is no return.

l: sage, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The sage is a person who renounces pleasure and possessions, lives wisely and humbly without worldly wishes or attachment, and does not kill living beings. Restrained and indifferent to worldly matters, the sage treats the gross body roughly, crosses the flood of life and samsara, and becomes liberated by ceasing from acts.

l: fool, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The fool is a worldly-minded person who longs for life, wealth, pleasures, and goods. Through ignorance and carelessness, he has much wrath and greed, performs injurious, cruel, or sinful deeds, does not know law, and comes to grief. Near death and far from liberation, he remains in the whirl of pains or births and cannot reach the opposite shore.

l: mortal people, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Mortal people, small beside gods, suffer through carelessness, labor, desire, violence, worldly attachment, and wealth; even their relations cannot ultimately protect them.

l: Sramanas, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: raise discussion [in this world] Some Sramanas raise the discussion that living beings may be slain, treated with violence, abused, tormented, or driven away without wrong.

l: women, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Women are portrayed as objects of worldly happiness that bring men pain, delusion, death, hell, and rebirth. They are also called the greatest temptation for sense-affected monks, who are instructed to avoid speaking of, seeing, conversing with, claiming, working for, and mentally dwelling on them.

l: attachment, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_overcome_by desirelessness [in the houseless life] Attachment to wealth, women, possessions, and pleasures causes delusion, suffering, and continued samsara. Those freed from attachment reach the opposite shore.

l: passions, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Passions are to be subdued through desirelessness and hard control: desire for wealth, pleasures, life, and worldly goods brings suffering and violence, while lust makes people sensual, cowardly, and attached to life, causing their decline.

l: sensual enjoyment, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Pleasure is difficult to reject and dear to fools; worldly attachment brings delusion, loss brings grief, and it unfolds into death and continued suffering.

l: wealth and treasures, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Wealth and treasures are desired so intensely that people commit injuries and violence; they may then be divided among heirs, stolen, taken by the king, ruined, or consumed by fire.

l: law, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The law is pure, unchangeable, and eternal, applying throughout the world to every kind of person. Taught by noble ones and known by sages, it calls for religious life while youth, health, and perceptions endure, through renunciation, control, non-killing, and freedom from possessions. The self-possessed, wise, just, chaste, careful, and zealous understand it correctly. They follow it to overcome Mâra and sinfulness, learn restraint and repentance, avoid harming living beings, and ultimately reach final liberation.

l: doctrine and faith, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The doctrine and faith is the highest doctrine declared for men by Mahâvîra, known and seen with quick discernment. It is a safe refuge for those in danger and opposes sin through avoidance. It begins with control, renunciation, non-killing, and true faith; continues through chastity, self-control, abandonment of worldliness, and harmless teaching; and ends in vows, restraint, tranquility, freedom from attachment, and final liberation.

l: violence, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Violence is an act by mortal people, done deliberately, from fear, for expiation or other hopes, and for special objects. It supports obligations yet causes unrighteousness and suffering. A wise man neither commits, orders, nor consents to it; understanding it reveals freedom from it.

l: non-killing, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_a true knowledge [joined with renunciation] Non-killing is perfectly known by the wise man who searches after liberation for the bound. The hero is not polluted by the sin of killing.

l: carelessness, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: shortens life [through injurious conduct] Carelessness causes people to desire wealth, commit violence, experience bodily and worldly suffering, and undergo repeated births. The text repeatedly urges people to cease from carelessness.

l: life, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: resembles dewdrop [for a slow and ignorant fool] Life fades through youth, age, sickness, and the deterioration of the senses. All beings are said to hold life dear and long to live.

l: death, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Death is an unavoidable, inescapable condition for mortal people, with nothing secure from it. It may come before religious life and is remembered calmly to overcome carelessness and worldly pleasure. It arises within a sequence linked to delusion, conception, hell, animal existence, pain, and repeated birth among those seized by Time and karman. Religious people seek liberation from death, while the sage who has reached the other side desires it as the dissolution of the body.

l: birth and death, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Birth and death are described as a continuing cycle that afflicts unenlightened people. The records urge knowledge of beings’ origins and destinations and steadfast right conduct; through this understanding, a person leaves the road of birth and death, rejoices in liberation, and reaches a state beyond speculation.

l: opposite shore, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_reached_by those freed from attachment [to the world and its pleasures] Those freed from attachment reach the opposite shore. The deluded and careless do not reach it, even when they hear the doctrine.

l: the body, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The body is loathsome within and without, painful, fragile, decaying, unstable, transient, and changeable. The informed person recognizes its foul interior humors and renounces attachment. Yet it is difficult to attain and offers an opportunity for liberation, making it worth preserving. Nourishment increases it and hardship makes it frail; an ascetic should care for and regulate it without attachment, endure pain, practice self-discipline, and dissolve it through exertion and reduced food.

l: path to final liberation, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The path to final liberation is a road followed by the wise, hero, and sage through right conduct, control, renunciation, non-killing, desirelessness, knowledge, and freedom from property and worldly ideas. Those who exert themselves cross life’s flood; attachment to sensual objects prevents arrival.

l: Third Lecture, Called Hot and Cold, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_a lecture It teaches restraint, nonviolence, knowledge of the world, and freedom from karman. It explains how conquering passions and avoiding sinful acts leads away from misery, death, and samsâra.

l: Nirgrantha, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Nirgrantha is a person equanimous toward heat, cold, pleasure, and pain, so unattached that he does not feel penance’s austerity.

l: Mâra, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_avoided_by man [through upright conduct and disregard of sensual objects] Mâra is avoided by the upright and is overcome by the wise man who exerts himself in the rule of truth.

l: Gainas, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Gainas are associated with a religion teaching control, non-killing, liberation, and contrasting the sage’s view of the world with the fool’s.

l: Tîrthakaras, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The Tîrthakaras are great heroes whose teaching is learned through an âkârya, innate knowledge, highest instruction, or others. Their commandment must not be broken. In former years they walked long and bore religious troubles, becoming perfected in knowledge and physically lean.

l: nonviolence, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Nonviolence, the opposite of violence, is understood by examining violence and adopting its contrary. It requires not injuring living beings, including through others or support for killing, and unfolds in Mahâvîra’s careful avoidance of harm while acting and begging.

l: misery, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Misery results from action, sensual attachment, and the course of the world. Understanding misery leads the wise to restraint, religious life, and freedom.

l: pleasure and pain, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_known_by monk [in their various forms] Pain and pleasure occur in various forms, and men suffer for their own sins. The zealous person understands their individual nature and does not turn aside from the aim of liberation.

l: birth, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: leads_to death [through the worldly chain] Birth is part of the chain connected with conception, death, hell, animal existence, and pain. Those influenced by karman are born again.

l: religious life, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Religious life is entered after seeing suffering, to avoid misery and seek a pious end and liberation. It is led carefully through restraint, circumspection, truth, guarded conduct, obedience, repentance, detachment, meditation, renunciation, and endurance. It unfolds from recognizing sinful action’s danger to sustained disciplined practice, exemplified by Mahâvîra’s years without cold water and in difficult resting-places.

l: truth, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Truth is to be followed constantly amid manifold sinful actions. A wise person delighting in it destroys all karman; through unrivalled control of the Gainas it is followed by Brahman, and heroes establish themselves in it with knowledge, exertion, and equanimity.

l: highest good, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The highest good is known by learned people and sages through right intuition, guiding a calm, guarded, restrained religious life free from sin.

l: passions, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The passions include wrath, pride, deceit, greed, love, hate, and delusion; conquering or avoiding one entails many.

l: doctrine of the Seer, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The doctrine of the Seer teaches non-injury and ending acts and samsâra; by preventing sin, it destroys former actions and karman, revealing the Seer without worldly weakness.

l: Fourth Lecture, Called Righteousness, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_a lecture The Fourth Lecture, Called Righteousness, teaches nonviolence toward all living beings, restraint from worldly motives, understanding of karman, and progress toward liberation.

l: Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present, and future, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: declare the pure, unchangeable, eternal law [universally] The Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present, and future declare that all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, treated with violence, abused, tormented, or driven away.

l: âsravas, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_as_many_as parisravas There are as many âsravas as there are parisravas. Understanding these categories helps the wise regard the world according to the instruction.

l: parisravas, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: There are as many parisravas as there are âsravas. They are considered together with âsravas in understanding the world.

l: anâsravas, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_as_many_as aparisravas There are as many anâsravas as there are aparisravas. They form part of the distinctions by which the wise understand the world.

l: aparisravas, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: There are as many aparisravas as there are anâsravas. They are explained as corresponding to anâsravas.

l: Brâhmanas, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: raise discussion [in this world] Some Brâhmanas raise the discussion that living beings may be slain, treated with violence, abused, tormented, or driven away without wrong.

l: the professors, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The professors affirm that pain is unpleasant for all living beings; being conversant with pain, they preach renunciation.

l: the wise ones, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: say that cruelty should be rejected [in this world] The wise ones speak about the consequences of actions and the distinctions between âsravas, parisravas, anâsravas, and aparisravas. They are described as discerning and as recognizing that pain results from actions.

l: the teachers, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: teach nonviolence [as their doctrine] The teachers reject the claim that harming living beings is without wrong and declare that all sorts of living beings should not be slain, treated with violence, abused, tormented, or driven away. They call this their doctrine.

l: renunciation, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Renunciation is preached by professors conversant with pain and practiced by wise, unattached people who know karman. It means leaving the world, possessions, and passions; living as a mendicant; and bearing disagreeable feelings to give up sinfulness and attain liberation. Mahâvîra exemplifies it by abandoning robe, shelter, food, treatment, and attachments, wandering naked and houseless.

l: bondage, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: flows_from external objects [along with cruel death and dreadful pain] Bondage flows from the source that also brings cruel death and dreadful pain. The discerning one cuts off that source and ceases to act.

l: freedom from acts, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_known_by the knower of the sacred lore [among mortals] Freedom from acts is known by the person who sees that acts will bear fruit and parts from karman. The discerning one recognizes and pursues this freedom.

l: the Seer, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: has no worldly weakness [none exists] The Seer has no worldly weakness. The text states that none exists in the Seer.

l: the sacred lore, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
